> 萃。亨。王假有廟，利見大人，亨，利貞。用大牲吉，利有攸往。

Hexagram 45 is about gathering, and its character comes from grass.

## 萃 is 從艸，卒聲

說文: 萃，艸貌 — the look of grass. 從艸，卒聲: phonetic, with 艸 as the semantic side.

Original sense: grass growing thick, in a patch.

And that original sense is the important part. Grass does not get planted one stalk at a time; it comes up as a patch by itself.

So 萃's "gathering" carries, from the beginning, the sense of gathering naturally — not of convening.

(A tally worth keeping: 萃 is the tenth character in this series read as 會意 when it is 形聲 — 卒 is a sound, not "soldiers gathering." Ten instances, one habit.)

## 王假有廟

假 is 至, to arrive (Wang Bi). Not 假借.

廟 is 貌 — 說文: 廟，尊先祖貌也. You give your ancestors a face, and therefore a 廟.

And a detail in the wording: the judgement says 有廟, not 于廟. Not "went to the temple," but "there is a temple" — the emphasis is not on where he went. It is that there is a common place to return to.

## 用大牲

大牲 is the ox, the heaviest offering in the rites.

And 禴, in 六二, is the thinnest of the four seasonal sacrifices: the summer offering, new vegetables only, no animal.

孚乃利用禴 — with trust, even the thin offering gets through.

Read with the judgement's 用大牲吉, the pair defines the chapter's measure: the weight of the rite follows the season, and the sincerity of the heart cannot be hidden in either direction.

## 一握為笑

初六: 若號，一握為笑. 勿恤，往無咎.

Wang Bi: 一握，小之貌也 — a handful, meaning "small." The smallness of the laugh, not "clasping hands."

Later commentators read it as "shaking hands and making peace," which is smoother and does not match the old glosses. Wang Bi and Zhu Xi both have "a small appearance."

So: someone was crying out, and then a little laughter came up — not a laugh, a change of colour.

Which is more accurate and more moving than the handshake: when a heart turns back, it usually does not arrive at understanding all at once. First there is that small smile.

## 引吉

引: to draw, to lead (說文 引，開弓也, to draw a bow; extended to pull, to guide).

六二 引吉，無咎 — good fortune by being led in, not by forcing one's way in.

The whole measure of the line is in that character: a gathering needs someone to bring you. Without one, pushing in produces the next line's 嗟如 — sighing, with nothing gained.

## 齎咨涕洟

齎咨: an exclamation of sighing (Wang Bi). 涕洟: tears, and tears plus mucus — crying until the nose runs.

The top line weeps, and the verdict is 無咎.

Which is the honest end of a chapter about gatherings: the one who has nothing to gather with is allowed to weep, and it is not counted against him.

## 除戎器，戒不虞

The 象: 君子以除戎器，戒不虞 — put the weapons in order, and guard against what is not expected.

A gathering is exactly when the unexpected arrives. So the hexagram that begins with grass coming up in a patch ends with an inventory of weapons — and it is not a contradiction: a crowd is the place where both things happen.

## The test

Take the group you are assembling — a team, a board, a family gathering. Ask whether you are 萃 (something growing into a patch) or 聚 (something being convened), and then ask whether there is someone who can lead people in, or whether everyone is pushing.
